Chemicals Industry Disrupted as Workers Stage Nationwide Walkout

Production lines across Israel’s chemicals industry ground to a halt Tuesday as workers launched a nationwide strike over wage negotiations, leaving manufacturers and suppliers scrambling to manage mounting disruptions.

The walkout began early in the morning after talks between the Chemicals Workers’ Union and the Israeli Chemical Manufacturers Association (ICMA) broke down late Monday. The union, representing more than 14,000 workers across the nation’s production, logistics, and maintenance facilities, is demanding a 7% pay increase and improved overtime compensation. Industry employers have offered a 3% increase, citing rising operating costs.

“We have been patient, but the cost of living is soaring, and our members deserve fair compensation for their essential work,” said union chair Eliav Barak, addressing workers outside the main gates of the NegevChem plant in Dimona. “We are ready to return to the negotiating table, but only if management is willing to listen.”

The strike immediately affected major facilities in Haifa Bay, Ashdod, and Ramat Hovav, with several plants suspending operations entirely. According to the ICMA, daily output losses are already estimated at 5,000 tonnes of fertilizers, plastics, and industrial solvents. Industry analysts warn that if the strike continues beyond 48 hours, stockpiles of raw materials at downstream users could run low, potentially slowing local manufacturing.

“This is the most significant disruption to the chemicals sector we’ve seen in over a decade,” said Dr. Yael Siman-Tov, an analyst with the Tel Aviv Industrial Forum. “The chemicals industry is a backbone of many supply chains, and extended downtime will have a ripple effect on deliveries and export commitments.”

Several companies, including Galil Polymers and BlueStar Chemicals, confirmed they had ceased shipments to clients until further notice. “Our warehouses are full, but without workers, we cannot load or dispatch any goods,” said BlueStar spokesperson Shira Lavi.

ICMA president Moshe Even called for a swift resolution. “Every day of lost production costs millions of shekels and undermines Israel’s reputation as a reliable chemicals supplier,” he said. “We urge the union to return to negotiations as soon as possible.”

As of Tuesday evening, both sides remained at an impasse, with no new talks scheduled. Union officials pledged to maintain the strike until their demands are addressed.
